title: What is the grass?
hookLine: a child asks "what is the grass?" and the poet of Leaves of Grass can't answer any better
tomorrow: do I contradict myself? what does Whitman say next?

lines: EVERY GROWN-UP REACHES FOR A PHONE.
cards: A kid at dinner asks where the moon goes in the daytime, and every grown-up at the table reaches for a phone. Here's the odd part.
Whitman named his whole book after grass, and in section six of Song of Myself, "A child said What is the grass? fetching it to me with full hands."
The poet of Leaves of Grass answers: "I do not know what it is any more than he." So why put that admission in the middle of his biggest poem?

teach.b: Because the not-knowing is where the poem opens. He doesn't fake an answer.

teach.h: THE FLAG, THE HANDKERCHIEF, A CHILD.
teach.b: He guesses out loud, the way you'd think with a child beside you. Maybe it's "the flag of my disposition, out of hopeful green stuff woven."
Maybe it's the handkerchief of the Lord, dropped on purpose, with the owner's name somewhere in the corners. Maybe the grass is itself a child. Then the guessing goes somewhere harder.
"And now it seems to me the beautiful uncut hair of graves." Grass grows out of the dead: the old, mothers, young men. And there the puzzle turns.
"The smallest sprout shows there is really no death."
Everything moves on: "All goes onward and outward, nothing collapses, And to die is different from what any one supposed, and luckier."

That's the teaching of section six: honest not-knowing, then patient looking, until even the hardest fact, death, shows up inside the growing world, not outside it. Whitman doesn't lay out a heaven here.
He looks at grass on a grave and reads life going on. And it starts with an honest sentence an adult can say to a child: I don't know either. Let's look.

how: Some readers of Whitman turn to section six of Song of Myself at funerals, in grief, or when a child asks about death, and read the grass passage aloud.

games.q: at a picnic, a seven-year-old holds up a wilted dandelion: why do flowers die? you're tempted to bluff. what fits section six?
o: say you don't know either, then guess out loud together and keep looking.
give one quick, firm answer so the question doesn't linger.
say it's too sad to talk about and point her to the swings.
games.why: that's Whitman's move: an honest I don't know, then guesses, then looking, until the grass itself says something about life going on.

practice: Choose a question a child once asked you, or one you asked as a kid and never got answered. Write it at the top of a page, and under it: I do not know. Then, slowly, write two honest guesses, the way Whitman did with the grass.

wordCard.voice: What is the grass? A child's question, the poet's honest I don't know, and the guesses that lead him to life going on, even out of graves.

carryVoice: One question to keep: what is the grass, where honest looking starts, beside a child with full hands. Back tomorrow.
